prompt: How does `Rect` come to satisfy `Shape` in section 02's program?
hint: Look at what the `Rect` declaration says, and what it does not.

choices.text: Its declaration ends in `implements Shape`
choices.why: Go has no such word; it is not among the 25 keywords, and `Rect` names no interface.

choices.text: It has a method `Area() float64`
choices.why: Right. `Area() float64` is the one method `Shape` lists, and having it is the whole of it.

choices.text: It is declared in the same package as `Shape`
choices.why: `time.Duration` satisfied an interface written in another package, in section 03.

choices.text: It embeds `Shape` as a field, as lesson 16 embedded structs
choices.why: `Rect` has only `W` and `H`; nothing is embedded in it.

prompt: `*os.File` writes `Write(b []byte) (n int, err error)` and `*strings.Builder` writes `Write(p []byte) (int, error)`. Which change to a type's `Write` would stop it satisfying `io.Writer`?
hint: Which parts of a signature did the two differ in, and still both fit?

choices.text: Calling the parameter `data` instead of `p`
choices.why: `*os.File` calls it `b` and fits; parameter names are documentation.

choices.text: Leaving the results without names
choices.why: `*strings.Builder` does exactly that and fits.

choices.text: Returning `(int64, error)`
choices.why: Right. The types of the results must match, and `int64` is not `int`.

choices.text: Declaring it in a file that does not import `io`
choices.why: The file declaring `strings.Builder` imports no `io` at all, and the builder fits.

prompt: In `fmt.Printf("%T", s)`, the verb `%T` prints the ___ of the value stored in the interface `s`.
hint: It printed `main.Rect` and `main.Circle`.

prompt: `buf` is a `bytes.Buffer` and `sb` a `strings.Builder`. Which can be the first argument of `fmt.Fprintf`? Choose all that apply.
hint: The parameter is an `io.Writer`, and the `Write` methods have pointer receivers except one.

choices.text: `os.Stdout`
choices.why: Yes. It is an `*os.File`, and the first line went straight to the terminal.

choices.text: `&buf`
choices.why: Yes. `*bytes.Buffer` has `Write` in its method set.

choices.text: `&sb`
choices.why: Yes, and it is how section 02 passed the builder.

choices.text: `sb`
choices.why: Refused: `Write` has a pointer receiver, so a `strings.Builder` value does not have it, as section 04 printed.

prompt: In section 02's program you delete the `Shape` type and `describe`, and the lines of `main` that used them. What happens to `Rect` and `Circle`?
hint: Where in their declarations does `Shape` appear?

choices.text: They stop compiling until their `Area` methods are removed too
choices.why: A method needs no interface to exist; `Area` is an ordinary method of each struct.

choices.text: Nothing: they compile unchanged, because they never referred to it
choices.why: Right. The relationship lived only where a value was used as a `Shape`.

choices.text: They compile, but `Area` can no longer be called on them
choices.why: `r.Area()` is a call on a `Rect`; it never went through `Shape`.

choices.text: The compiler reports that they implement nothing
choices.why: A type is never required to satisfy an interface, so there is nothing to report.

prompt: Why does an interface with one method fit more types than one with ten?
hint: What must a type have before it fits?

choices.text: The compiler checks small interfaces less strictly
choices.why: Every method is checked the same way; `Grid` failed `Shape`, which has one.

choices.text: A type needs every listed method, and one is easy to have
choices.why: Right. Each method added is one more thing a type must have before it fits.

choices.text: One-method interfaces are satisfied by every type automatically
choices.why: Only by types that have that method; a `Rect` is not an `io.Reader`.

choices.text: Go limits the types that may satisfy a large interface
choices.why: There is no such limit; a large interface is simply harder to have all of.

prompt: `countWords` is changed to take an `*os.File` instead of an `io.Reader`. Which of its three calls stops compiling?
hint: What type is `os.Stdin`?

choices.text: The call with `os.Stdin`, because a pipe is not a file
choices.why: `os.Stdin` is an `*os.File`, whatever is connected to it.

choices.text: The call with `strings.NewReader(...)`
choices.why: Right. It is a `*strings.Reader`, and the string would have to be written to a file first.

choices.text: All three, because `bufio.NewScanner` only takes an `io.Reader`
choices.why: An `*os.File` is an `io.Reader`, so passing `f` on to the scanner still compiles.

choices.text: None: Go converts each argument to `*os.File`
choices.why: Go converts nothing implicitly, lesson 10, and a `*strings.Reader` cannot become a file.

prompt: Why does `os.Open` return an `*os.File` and not an `io.Reader`?
hint: What did the program do with `f` after counting?

choices.text: The caller keeps `Close` and the rest, and `f` still fits `io.Reader`
choices.why: Right. A concrete result costs nothing, and `f` went to `countWords` as an `io.Reader`.

choices.text: An interface cannot be returned from a function, so a concrete type is the one option
choices.why: It can; `io.MultiWriter` returns a `Writer`. Returning the concrete type is a choice.

choices.text: An `*os.File` is faster to read from than any `io.Reader` would be
choices.why: The same `Read` runs either way; what changes is which methods the caller can see.

choices.text: `os` was written before `io` existed
choices.why: `os.Open`'s file already has a `Read` that fits `io.Reader`; the order of history is not the reason.

prompt: Match each habit to where section 03 showed it.
hint: Three habits, three programs.

pairs.left: accept the smallest interface you need
return the concrete type you have
declare the interface where it is used

prompt: You write `save(dst ..., r Report) error`, and it only ever calls `dst.Write` and `dst.Close`. What type should `dst` have?
hint: Ask for exactly what the function calls.

choices.text: `*os.File`, since a report usually ends up in a file
choices.why: Then a caller with a buffer or a network connection could not use it; `countWords` showed the cost.

choices.text: `io.ReadWriteCloser`, to be safe in case `save` ever needs to read back
choices.why: It asks for `Read` too, which `save` never calls, and shuts out every writer that cannot read.

choices.text: An interface with `Write` and `Close`, such as `io.WriteCloser`
choices.why: Right. Two methods are called, so two are asked for, and nothing more.

choices.text: `any`, so that anything at all can be passed
choices.why: `any` has no methods, so `dst.Write` would not compile; lesson 28 is about what `any` costs.

prompt: The compiler says `Square does not implement Shape (missing method Area)`. What is wrong with `Square`?
hint: Read the parenthesis.

choices.text: Its `Area` method returns the wrong type
choices.why: That message is `wrong type for method Area`, with `have` and `want` lines.

choices.text: Its `Area` method has a pointer receiver
choices.why: That message ends in `(method Area has pointer receiver)`.

choices.text: It does not say `implements Shape`
choices.why: No type says that in Go; `Rect` fitted without it.

choices.text: It has no method called `Area` at all
choices.why: Right. Its method is called `Size`, and the name has to match.

prompt: Whether a value fits an interface is checked where the value is used, and at ___ time, so a mismatch never reaches a running program.
hint: `go build` printed every one of section 04's errors.

prompt: `Grid` failed with `have Area() int` and `want Area() float64`. Which change makes it a `Shape`?
hint: Which line describes `Grid`, and which describes `Shape`?

choices.text: Write `Shape(g)` in the slice literal
choices.why: A conversion asks the same question and gets the same answer; the method still returns `int`.

choices.text: Make `Area` return a `float64`
choices.why: Right. `have` must become `want`: the result converted with `float64(...)` inside the method.

choices.text: Change `Shape` itself to `Area() int`
choices.why: `Grid` would fit, and every type returning `float64`, `Rect` and `Circle` among them, would stop fitting.

choices.text: Add a second method `Area() float64` beside the first
choices.why: A type cannot have two methods of one name; the compiler refuses the second.

prompt: `encoding/json` writes `var _ Marshaler = (*RawMessage)(nil)` and not `var _ Marshaler = RawMessage{}`. What does the pointer form allow?
hint: Which method set is larger?

choices.text: It makes the check run once at start-up instead of on every call
choices.why: Neither form runs a check at all while the program runs; the compiler makes it.

choices.text: It avoids allocating a `RawMessage`, which would fail the build
choices.why: Allocating breaks no build. What matters is which method set gets compared.

choices.text: The pointer's method set is compared, pointer methods included
choices.why: Right. A pointer's method set has both kinds; a nil one is the cheapest pointer to write.

choices.text: Nothing: the two lines check the same thing
choices.why: They differ exactly when a method has a pointer receiver, which is lesson 26's table.

prompt: A team's `Rect` is used as a `Shape` only in another package, `render`. Somebody renames `Area` to `Size` in `Rect`'s package. Without `var _ Shape = Rect{}`, where does the error appear?
hint: Section 04 built the renamed `Rect` on its own first.

choices.text: In `Rect`'s package, at the renamed method
choices.why: That package built and ran, printing 12; nothing in it used `Rect` as a `Shape`.

choices.text: In `render`, where a `Rect` is used as a `Shape`
choices.why: Right. The check happens at the use, so it fails for whoever owns the use; the blank line moves it home.

choices.text: Nowhere at all, until the program runs and finally calls `Area`
choices.why: Interface checks are made when building, never at run time.

choices.text: In the file that declares `Shape`
choices.why: `Shape` is unchanged and fine; an interface never lists the types that fit it.

prompt: Put in order what happens for `fmt.Fprintf(&sb, "hi")`, from compiling to running.
hint: The first two happen in `go build`.
items: `&sb`, a `*strings.Builder`, is passed where an `io.Writer` is asked for
the compiler finds `Write` in the method set of `*strings.Builder`
at run time, `Fprintf` formats `hi` into bytes
`Fprintf` calls `w.Write`, which runs the builder's own `Write`

prompt: With section 02's types, `shapes := []Shape{Rect{W: 1, H: 5}, Rect{W: 2, H: 3}}` and the loop that adds up `s.Area()`. What is the total?
hint: Each `Area` is the `Rect`'s own.

prompt: Package `report` declares `type source interface { Rows() [][]string }`. Package `db` has a type with that exact method and does not import `report`. Can a value of it be passed to `report`'s functions?
hint: Did `time` import the program that declared `labeler`?

choices.text: No: `db` has to import `report` to see the interface
choices.why: `time` never imported the program that declared `labeler`, and its types fitted.

choices.text: No, because `source` starts with a lower-case letter
choices.why: Lower case keeps other packages from naming `source`; it does not stop their values fitting it.

choices.text: Only through a conversion, `source(v)`, written in `db`
choices.why: `db` cannot even name `source`, and no conversion is needed where the value is passed.

choices.text: Yes: the method set fits, and nothing else is asked
choices.why: Right. The interface lives with its user, and the type never has to know it exists.

prompt: A program declares `type labeler interface { String() string }`. Which of these can be passed as a `labeler`? Choose all that apply.
hint: `go doc strings.Builder` listed `func (b *Builder) String() string`.

choices.text: `90 * time.Minute`
choices.why: Yes: a `time.Duration` has `String`, and printed `1h30m0s`.

choices.text: `&sb`, where `sb` is a `strings.Builder`
choices.why: Yes: `*strings.Builder` has `String() string`, with a pointer receiver.

choices.text: `sb` itself
choices.why: No: `String` is a pointer method, so the value lacks it; lesson 26's `Money` failed the same way.

choices.text: `Rect{W: 3, H: 4}` from section 02
choices.why: No: `Rect` has `Area` and no `String`.

prompt: A library adds a method `Close() error` to one of its types in a new release. Which interfaces does the type satisfy from then on?
hint: Nothing in the type lists interfaces.

choices.text: None new, until the library declares which ones it implements
choices.why: There is nothing to declare in Go; having the method is the declaration.

choices.text: Every interface whose methods it now all has, wherever it is declared
choices.why: Right. Satisfaction is checked against the method set, wherever an interface is used.

choices.text: Only `io.Closer`, the one interface named after that method
choices.why: A program's own `type closer interface { Close() error }` fits as well; names of interfaces are not matched.

choices.text: Only the interfaces declared inside that library
choices.why: `time.Duration` fitted `labeler`, which `time` has never seen.
